question: You committed a note locally, but your branch on GitHub has not changed. What normally sends the commit to GitHub?

explanations.A: Fetch downloads remote information.
explanations.B: Push sends local commits to the remote.
explanations.C: Status reports local state.
explanations.D: Add selects content for a commit.

key_idea: Commit is local; push shares commits.

question: You want to download remote history before deciding how to integrate it. Which command fits?

explanations.A: Pull also integrates according to its options.
explanations.C: Fetch downloads remote history without merging it into your checked-out branch.
explanations.D: Init creates a local repository.

key_idea: Fetch lets you inspect before integration.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes Git from GitHub?

options.A: Git tracks versions; GitHub hosts repositories and collaboration tools.
options.B: Git requires GitHub for every commit.
options.C: GitHub is the name of the Git staging area.
options.D: Git and GitHub are interchangeable names.

explanations.A: Git works locally and GitHub adds hosted collaboration.
explanations.B: A local commit does not require GitHub.
explanations.C: The staging area belongs to Git.
explanations.D: They are different tools with connected uses.

key_idea: Local version control can exist without a hosting account.

question: A new reader needs setup instructions for this project. Which file is the best starting point?

explanations.A: CODEOWNERS maps paths to owners.
explanations.C: SECURITY describes reporting security concerns.
explanations.D: README introduces the project and explains how to use it.

key_idea: README is the project entry point.

question: Which file identifies people or teams responsible for particular repository paths?

explanations.A: CODEOWNERS maps file patterns to owners.
explanations.C: A stash holds temporary local work.
explanations.D: A Project view organizes tracked items.

key_idea: Ownership mapping is separate from review enforcement.

question: A repository is public and has no license file. Which conclusion is appropriate?

options.B: Its reuse permissions need to be checked; public visibility is not an open-source license.
options.C: Starring it gives you a commercial license.

explanations.A: Visibility alone does not grant unrestricted reuse.
explanations.B: Public access and licensing answer different questions.
explanations.C: A star does not grant licensing rights.
explanations.D: A fork does not erase the original terms or rights.

key_idea: Visibility is not a license.

question: You want maintainers to review a branch change before integrating it. What should you open?

explanations.A: A gist shares a snippet.
explanations.C: A PR proposes a change for discussion and review.
explanations.D: A star saves or signals interest in a repository.

key_idea: A PR is a proposal to integrate a change.

question: A PR description says Closes #12. Under the normal keyword behavior, when does the referenced issue close?

options.B: When the PR is merged into the default branch

explanations.A: Staging is local Git work.
explanations.B: The default-branch merge triggers the closing relationship.
explanations.C: Stars do not close linked issues.
explanations.D: Cloning does not trigger issue closure.

key_idea: Link the issue and merge to the correct branch.

question: You need a simple static documentation website from repository content. Which feature fits?

explanations.A: Stash stores local work.
explanations.C: Notifications communicate activity.
explanations.D: Pages hosts static site content.

key_idea: Pages publishes a static site.

question: You need a hosted development environment with a terminal to execute tests. Which option fits?

explanations.A: A board tracks work.
explanations.C: Codespaces supplies a hosted development environment with compute.
explanations.D: A star does not supply execution tools.

key_idea: Codespaces can run tools, not just edit text.

question: In an Actions workflow, what is a runner?

options.A: The machine that executes a job
options.B: The title of a pull request
options.D: The person who starred a repository

explanations.A: A runner provides the execution environment for a job.
explanations.C: A license describes reuse terms.
explanations.D: Starring does not define a runner.

key_idea: The runner executes the job.

question: Copilot suggests a fix and generated tests. What is the best next step?

options.C: Assume the tests ran in chat
options.D: Review the changes and run appropriate tests

explanations.A: Generated code can be incorrect.
explanations.C: Generating test text is not proof of execution.
explanations.D: Review and execution provide evidence about the proposal.

key_idea: AI suggestions still need verification.

question: You want to see the same Project items in columns and in rows. What should you use?

options.B: Board and table views of the same Project

explanations.A: Repositories are not needed to change a Project layout.
explanations.B: Views present the same items in different layouts.
explanations.C: Forks copy repositories, not layout settings.
explanations.D: License files do not control views.

key_idea: A view changes presentation, not the underlying work.

question: Your issue closed but its board item stayed In Progress. What should you check first?

options.C: The Project workflow that updates Status on issue closure

explanations.A: Local Git installation does not set this Project automation.
explanations.C: The workflow controls the intended status update.
explanations.D: Stars do not drive this workflow.

key_idea: Issue state and Project Status are separate unless connected by automation.

question: What is the main purpose of a GitHub Project?

options.A: Plan and track work using issues, PRs, and fields

explanations.A: Projects organize and visualize work.
explanations.B: Git history remains in the repository.
explanations.C: Projects are not a password vault.
explanations.D: A Project does not provide code execution.

key_idea: Planning tools organize work; they do not replace version control.

question: A contributor needs to organize issues and PRs without pushing code. Which common repository role fits?

explanations.A: Admin is broader than the stated task.
explanations.B: Write includes code contribution capabilities beyond this need.
explanations.C: Triage supports issue and PR management without code write access.
explanations.D: Organization ownership is much broader.

key_idea: Match access to the task.

question: What makes an organization team different from a personal repository collaborator?

options.A: Teams can only contain outside collaborators.
options.B: Teams group organization members and can receive repository access together.
options.C: Teams automatically make every repository public.
options.D: A Project board creates organization membership.

explanations.A: Outside collaborators cannot belong to organization teams.
explanations.C: A team does not automatically change repository visibility.
explanations.D: Project tracking does not create organization membership.

key_idea: Team membership belongs to an organization.

question: Who can read a secret gist if its URL is shared with them?

options.A: Only the author under all circumstances
options.C: Only users with write access to a separate repository

explanations.A: Secret gists are not private.
explanations.C: A separate repository role is not the access condition.
explanations.D: The URL can expose an unlisted gist to others.

key_idea: Unlisted does not mean access-controlled.

question: You want to contribute to a project where you cannot push branches. Which route fits?

options.A: Fork, make a branch change, and propose a PR
options.D: Star the project to receive write access

explanations.A: A fork supports proposing a contribution without upstream write access.
explanations.B: Sharing passwords is not a contribution workflow.
explanations.C: Visibility is not yours to change and does not grant write access.
explanations.D: Stars do not grant permissions.

key_idea: A fork lets you prepare a contribution under your own account.

question: Where can you discover reusable Actions and GitHub apps?

explanations.A: A stash holds local changes.
explanations.C: Marketplace lists Actions and apps.
explanations.D: A gist is not the product catalog.

key_idea: Marketplace helps discover integrations.

question: Before submitting a first contribution, what should you inspect?

options.B: The project contribution guidance and relevant issue context

explanations.A: Popularity does not explain contribution expectations.
explanations.B: Guidance and issue context help you propose useful work.
explanations.C: Credentials are unnecessary and private.
explanations.D: Your profile does not explain project requirements.

key_idea: Read the project expectations before proposing a change.
